chapter: Bill Robinson and Chuck and Chuckles
title: Bill Robinson the sport and amateur-contest runner
summary: Green says Robinson was a track star who won contests across theatres and kept the tap dancers' history with Dudley; he carried a police gift pistol.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and the Prohibition-era clubs

blocks.x: Well, he was a sport. He was a very happy personality, a great personality. He was a track star too, and his work, which was tap dancing, became like what you would call a relay runner on a track, passing the stick and so on, steeplechasing or whatever, and he could do 26 different tap dance dances. So he got discovered by some millionaire, happened to see him. He used to go around and from one theater amateur contest to the other theater's amateur contest, so that way he would get a chance to do about four shows a day, you see? And if he didn't win one amateur contest, he'd probably win the other one, you see? As long as he'd at least win one or two, you see. And that's how he developed his tap dancing, because he was applying new degrees to the art itself. See, they had to make book on the history of the tap dancers. That was Mr. Dudley, the owner of the Hoofer's Club, that's what he did, because they were his favorite performers, the tap dancers. And that's really why Mr. Buddy Bradley and Mr. Dudley was kind of -- they were very well acquainted and they had been co-workers, see. And --
